thread.title: Apple Changed the Way It Reports iPhone Sales and It Could Be Good News for the Stock

title: Apple Changed the Way It Reports iPhone Sales and It Could Be Good News for the Stock
text:
Apple Changed the Way It Reports iPhone Sales and It Could Be Good News for the Stock By Updated Nov. 5, 2018 2:01 p.m. ET Order Reprints Photograph by Greg Baker/AFP/Getty Images Text size
“ Apple Reduces Disclosure; Typically Not a Good Sign,” wrote one analyst about the iPhone maker’s latest quarterly earnings report . And that about sums it up. Last Thursday, Apple beat estimates for revenue and earnings, reported just OK guidance for the Christmas quarter and said it will no longer break out iPhone sales going forward. This last item, in particular, seemed to rankle investors. Apple stock (AAPL) tumbled almost 7% on Friday, and kept falling on Monday . Apple stock is now down about 10% since the report.
One reading of Apple’s shift on disclosure, after all, is that Apple has so successfully saturated the globe with high-priced smartphones that it will struggle to grow unit sales from here, and would rather not point that out for investors each quarter. Consider another interpretation, however: Apple wants investors to focus on its earnings, not its units, because steady, rising earnings are the path to a higher stock valuation. The best remote control you have is the one in your pocket. As long as you have the right apps—and you'll need a lot of them—you can control almost everything on your TV right from your iPhone or Android smartphone. WSJ's David Pierce shows you how to set it all up. Photo/Video: Emily Prapuolenis/The Wall Street Journal
Quarterly reporting time, after all, hasn’t generally been much fun for Apple in recent years, even as it has continued flourishing. Barron’s turned positive on Apple back in spring 2014 at about $76, split-adjusted. Shares recently changed hands at $200. Yearly earnings per share have more than doubled since that story, and the stock valuation rebounded from a broken-down 13 times earnings to about 15 times. Even so, Apple stock has fallen after eight of the company’s past 15 quarterly reports. The average decline has been 4% in a day. Clearly, Apple doesn’t have much to lose by shaking up the way it reports results to investors.
Read more : Apple Stock Is Tumbling and That’s Good News — for Fund Managers
There’s more to it, however. As we have written in recent years, Apple is moving beyond boom-and-bust cycles for phone upgrades to a steadier earnings trajectory. One reason is that fast-growing sales of high-margin services are offsetting a slowdown in iPhone unit sales. In fact, based on a statistical measurement of earnings volatility, Apple now compares favorably with consumer-staples companies .
Staples sellers tend to trade at higher valuations for their safety. Comparing electronics with, say, food might be a stretch, but then again, which would an average consumer be more likely to switch away from: his Cheerios or his iPhone? Packaged-food makers have been struggling with price pressure from a grocery war and shoppers buying more fresh food. For Apple, retention rates are exceptionally high and prices have been rising.
If Apple can get investors to focus less on how its quarterly iPhone volumes compare with guesses, and more on bottom-line results, it could be viewed less as a hit-or-miss gadget maker and more as a digital staple seller.
“No doubt it will take time for the Street to digest this new chapter for Apple, but ultimately we believe it will translate into a higher multiple over the next few years (above its traditional 12x-16x P/E ratio),” wrote Wedbush Securities analyst Daniel Ives in a Monday note to investors. With Apple having an installed base of 1.3 billion devices sold to date, Ives reckons services revenue–cloud storage, extended warranties, app sales and so on–will grow by 20% a year from here and reach $50 billion by fiscal 2020. He estimates that Apple’s services alone are worth $400 billion to $450 billion. If the right number is anywhere close to that, Apple’s overall stock market value, now just under $1 trillion, looks modest.
